messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The flood came at night, a wall of water that ripped through the small town where Marco had been stationed as a military medic. He had spent fourteen hours pulling people from the wreckage, working in the dark with a headlamp and his bare hands. What stayed with him was not the water itself but the sounds—the way the timber groaned and snapped, the screams that suddenly cut off, the silence afterward that was worse than any noise. Now, forty-five years old and three years widowed, Marco lived alone in a ground-floor apartment in a city that had never flooded. He had left the service, taken a job as a paramedic dispatcher, a desk job where he could help without being in the field. But the sounds followed him. A car backfiring outside the dispatch center would send him out of his chair, heart hammering, scanning the room for exits. He had come to believe that the world was a place where safety could be erased in an instant, and that belief had hollowed him out.

Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. Marco could not put the memories of that night in the right order—the images came in fragments, a child’s shoe floating past, the cold feel of a wrist that had no pulse, the roar of water that seemed to come from everywhere at once. When the memory returned, he felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes right in the middle of a call at work, his supervisor touching his shoulder and asking if he was okay. The terror he had felt that night came back undiminished, as though no time had passed at all. And because he believed that his own life no longer had meaning, he saw these memories as further proof that he was broken, that the man who had once known who he was had been washed away along with everything else. He felt like he didn’t know himself anymore. His beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed.

The causal loop tightened over the months. The hypervigilance—being superalert and watchful and on guard at every unexpected sound—fed his conviction that the world was dangerous, which in turn made the memories more vivid and more frequent. He was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His own living room, with the deadbolt locked and the windows closed, felt like a staging area for disaster. He would sit on the edge of his couch, listening, waiting. And the more he watched for threat, the more he found evidence that threat was everywhere, which only deepened his sense that nothing mattered anymore. The lost meaning and the shattered beliefs made the memories worse, because every flashback confirmed that he was no longer the person he had been. And the memories, in turn, strengthened the appraisals: if he could not even keep his own mind in order, how could he ever feel whole again?

What finally brought Marco to seek help was not his own suffering but a mistake at work. He had misheard a dispatch address because a truck had rumbled past the window, and the ambulance had been sent to the wrong block. No one was hurt, but his supervisor had pulled him aside and asked if he needed to talk to someone. Marco had sat in his car in the parking lot for twenty minutes afterward, his hands shaking on the steering wheel, trying to remember the sequence of the flood—the order of things—and finding only noise. He was afraid that he would lose this job, the last thing that gave his days any shape. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never find his way back to the person he used to be, that the water had taken that too. But he made the appointment anyway, because for the first time in three years, he was more afraid of staying the same.
